mcqs.question: What's the actual mechanism behind a cache stampede?
options: The database silently corrupts data when too many reads happen at once
The cache entry expires, every concurrent reader misses at the same instant, and each independently queries the database to recompute the same value
The cache expiring causes application servers to crash outright
A stampede only happens when a key's TTL is set to exactly zero
mcqs.explanation: The mechanism is simple but important to state precisely: one expiry event turns into N independent database queries for the same value, all at once, because every one of the N concurrent readers misses the cache together and has no idea the others are doing the same query. There's no data corruption, no crash, and no dependency on a zero TTL.

mcqs.question: What does stale-while-revalidate actually do when a hot cache key expires?
options: It deletes the cached value immediately so every reader gets a guaranteed-fresh value
It disables caching entirely for that key until traffic drops
It keeps serving the old value to readers while exactly one background request refreshes it, so nobody sees a miss
It requires every reader to independently refresh the value in parallel
mcqs.explanation: Stale-while-revalidate trades a small amount of extra staleness for eliminating the miss entirely — readers keep getting an answer (the old one) while a single background refresh brings it current. Deleting on expiry is the opposite of this pattern, disabling caching defeats the purpose, and having every reader refresh in parallel is exactly the stampede this pattern avoids.

mcqs.question: Request coalescing is in place, but the database is still overwhelmed because many different hot keys expire around the same time. What else would you add?
options: Increase coalescing to allow up to 10 simultaneous queries per key instead of 1
Add more read replicas so more simultaneous queries can be absorbed
Remove the TTL entirely so keys never expire again
A fleet-wide distributed lock so only one process across all nodes refreshes a given key, and/or probabilistic early refresh so refreshes spread out before the TTL boundary
mcqs.explanation: Per-key coalescing only limits queries to one per node — a fleet-wide lock closes the gap across nodes, and probabilistic early refresh prevents many different keys from all hitting their expiry moment together. Loosening coalescing reintroduces the very problem it fixes, more replicas just raises the ceiling without addressing the pile-up pattern, and removing the TTL trades the stampede for permanently stale data.

mcqs.question: After a stampede takes down the database, a team's fix is "scale the database up." What's the flaw in stopping there?
options: It treats the database overload as the problem, when the actual cause is many identical requests recomputing the same value at once — scaling the DB just raises the threshold where the same stampede recurs
It's a fine fix as long as the database is scaled by at least 10x
Scaling the database is always the correct first response to any cache-related issue
Stampedes only happen on databases that don't support read replicas
mcqs.explanation: Scaling the database addresses the symptom, not the mechanism — the same stampede pattern recurs at whatever the new, higher traffic threshold is, since nothing about many requests recomputing the same value has changed. There's no scaling factor that fixes this instead of just deferring it, and it's not the correct first response when the actual fix (coalescing, staggered expiry) is cheaper and addresses the cause directly. Read-replica support is unrelated to whether a stampede can occur.
